name: Audio and Video Evidence
title: Audio and Video Evidence
answer: Audio and video evidence covers recorded speech, surveillance footage, body camera video, call recordings, voicemail, and meeting captures that become part of a legal matter. In e-discovery it sits alongside email and documents, but it is heavier, messier, and often far larger in volume. The work spans identification, collection, processing, review, and production of these recordings, usually under a court-ordered schedule. Practitioners in this area are litigators, paralegals, and forensic analysts rather than machine learning engineers.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Audio and video evidence covers recorded speech, surveillance footage, body camera video, call recordings, voicemail, and meeting captures that become part of a legal matter. In e-discovery it sits alongside email and documents, but it is heavier, messier, and often far larger in volume. The work spans identification, collection, processing, review, and production of these recordings, usually under a court-ordered schedule. Practitioners in this area are litigators, paralegals, and forensic analysts rather than machine learning engineers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The pipeline runs on capture devices, chain-of-custody storage, and processing platforms that transcode proprietary formats into reviewable files. Speech-to-text engines generate transcripts with timestamps and speaker labels, and computer vision models index faces, objects, and scenes in video. Review typically happens in e-discovery platforms that link a transcript line to the exact moment in the recording. Storage and compute costs dominate, because a single day of surveillance video can exceed the size of an entire document collection.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts first authenticate the file and preserve the original, then create a working copy for processing. Automatic transcription and speaker diarization produce a searchable text layer, and keyword or concept search narrows the set before human review. Reviewers watch or listen to flagged segments, correct transcript errors, and tag relevance, privilege, or confidentiality. Video review often uses frame-level or clip-level coding, and quality control checks compare the transcript against the audio before anything is produced.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Recordings raise consent, privacy, and wiretapping issues that vary by jurisdiction, and some material may be protected by privilege or subject to protective order. Provenance matters: courts expect a documented chain of custody, hashes of original files, and a record of every transformation applied. Transcripts produced by automated tools are treated as derivative work product and must be verified before use.Nothing here is legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Multimodal models that reason over audio, video, and text together are beginning to collapse the separate transcription and review steps into one pass. Real-time redaction of faces, voices, and personal identifiers is improving, which reduces the manual burden of producing sensitive recordings. Expect tighter integration between capture devices and review platforms, so that chain of custody is recorded automatically rather than reconstructed later. The open questions are accuracy claims, admissibility of machine-generated transcripts, and how courts will treat model output as evidence in its own right.
